name: Isabella I of Castile
info: Isabella I, known as Isabella the Catholic (1451–1504), was Queen of Castile and León from 1474 who, with her husband Ferdinand II of Aragon, conquered Granada, expelled Spain's Jews and sponsored Columbus's voyage of 1492.

facts.born: 22 April 1451 (Maundy Thursday) at Madrigal de las Altas Torres; daughter of King John II of Castile and of his second wife, Isabella of Portugal
facts.died: 26 November 1504 at the Royal Palace of Medina del Campo, of uterine cancer leading to dropsy; buried in the Capilla Real in Granada beside Ferdinand
facts.role: Princess and heir presumptive of Castile from 1468; Queen of Castile and León from 1474 to 1504; Queen of Aragon from 1479 as the wife of Ferdinand II; with Ferdinand, one of the Catholic Monarchs
facts.known: her marriage to Ferdinand of Aragon in 1469; winning the War of the Castilian Succession; the Santa Hermandad and her reforms of the crown's finances and council; the conquest of Granada, ending the Reconquista; sponsoring Christopher Columbus; the Alhambra Decree expelling the Jews; the Spanish Inquisition

t: Isabella won the throne of Castile through a civil war, a secret marriage to Ferdinand of Aragon in 1469 and the War of the Castilian Succession, ended at Alcáçovas in 1479.
With Ferdinand she restored royal finances and justice, conquered Granada in 1492, sponsored Columbus's voyage that year and so began the Spanish Empire.

Her policy of religious unity brought the Inquisition, the expulsion of the Jews in 1492 and the forced conversion of Muslims after 1502, and her cause for sainthood was suspended in 1991 over the expulsion.
dyk: In 1893 Isabella became the first woman featured on United States postage stamps and the first named woman on a United States coin, the Isabella quarter, both marking 400 years since Columbus's first voyage.
ev: Born at Madrigal de las Altas Torres, daughter of John II of Castile and Isabella of Portugal
At Toros de Guisando, her half-brother Henry IV names her his heir presumptive
Marries Ferdinand of Aragon in Valladolid without Henry's knowledge
Proclaimed Queen of Castile and León at Segovia after Henry IV's death
The treaties of Alcáçovas end the War of the Castilian Succession and secure her throne
Enters Granada with Ferdinand, issues the Alhambra Decree expelling the Jews and sponsors Columbus's first voyage
The Catholic Monarchs break the Treaty of Granada and order Muslims to become Christians or leave
Withdraws from government and dies at Medina del Campo

sections.early:
Isabella was born on 22 April 1451 at Madrigal de las Altas Torres, the daughter of King John II of Castile and his second wife, Isabella of Portugal. She stood second in line to the throne behind her childless half-brother Henry, and third after her brother Alfonso was born in 1453. When her father died in 1454 Henry became king as Henry IV, and Isabella, Alfonso and their mother moved to Arévalo, where they lived in poor conditions and short of money, for Henry did not pay what their father's will provided. Under her mother she was taught practical piety and a deep reverence for religion.

When Henry's queen, Joan of Portugal, was about to give birth to their daughter Joanna, Isabella and Alfonso were summoned to court at Segovia, and Isabella joined the queen's household. Her education there ranged from grammar, history, rhetoric and philosophy to French, Italian and Portuguese, music, needlework, riding, hunting and falconry, but Henry rarely let her leave Segovia. Her marriage was a question from childhood. At six she was betrothed to Ferdinand, younger son of John II of Navarre, but the alliance soon lapsed; a plan to marry her to Charles of Viana ended when his father imprisoned him. In 1465 she refused consent to a match with Afonso V of Portugal, and a betrothal to Pedro Girón, Master of Calatrava, ended when he fell ill and died on his way to meet her.
sections.rise:
In 1464 a faction of nobles led by Juan Pacheco and Alfonso Carrillo spread rumours that Henry's daughter Joanna was the child of the royal favourite Beltrán de la Cueva, and civil war broke out in 1465 after they deposed Henry in effigy outside Ávila and crowned Alfonso. When Alfonso died at fourteen in July 1468, his supporters suspecting poison, the nobles asked Isabella to lead the rebellion. She preferred a settlement: at Toros de Guisando Henry recognised her as heir presumptive on 19 September 1468, and she agreed not to marry without his consent, though he could not force a match on her. When Henry pressed marriages to Afonso V and to Charles, Duke of Berry, she refused and secretly promised herself to Ferdinand of Aragon. They were married at Valladolid on 19 October 1469 with a supposed papal bull of Pius II, who had died in 1464, obtained with the help of Cardinal Rodrigo Borgia. Henry disinherited her and in 1470 declared Joanna his heir.

Henry died on 11 December 1474, and on 13 December Isabella was proclaimed queen at Segovia. Supporters of Joanna married her to Afonso V of Portugal, who invaded in May 1475. At the Battle of Toro on 1 March 1476 both sides claimed victory, but Joanna's party broke up and the Portuguese withdrew. The treaties of Alcáçovas of 4 September 1479 confirmed Isabella's throne in exchange for almost all the disputed Atlantic territories except the Canary Islands and a large war indemnity.
sections.deeds:
Isabella found Castile in debt and disorder after Henry's reign. In 1476 she brought the local brotherhoods under the crown as the Santa Hermandad, a police force paid by a tax of 1,800 maravedís on every hundred households, and officials she sent to Galicia in 1481 drove out over 1,500 robbers. The Cortes of Toledo of 1480 resumed royal lands Henry had sold below their value, except gifts to churches, hospitals and the poor; she cut the mints, which had grown from five to 150, and fixed a standard for the coinage. The Royal Council was given to lawyers of the lesser nobility and bourgeoisie, the monarchs heard complaints in person on Fridays, and the jurist Alfonso Díaz de Montalvo compiled the Ordenanzas Reales.

In 1482 the Catholic Monarchs began the war against the Nasrid Emirate of Granada, the last Muslim state of the peninsula. With soldiers from many countries and the best artillery, they took Ronda in 1485, Málaga, and Baza in 1489, and on 2 January 1492 entered Granada, whose principal mosque was made a church; the Treaty of Granada promised its Muslims and Jews peace. Three months later Isabella agreed to sponsor Christopher Columbus, who sailed on 3 August 1492 and reached the New World on 12 October. The Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494 divided the world beyond Europe with Portugal. In 1492 she also endorsed Antonio de Nebrija's grammar of the Castilian language, which Nebrija meant to teach to the peoples of the new lands.
sections.opponents:
Isabella and Ferdinand pursued religious and national unity through the Inquisition, with the Dominican Tomás de Torquemada as the first Inquisitor General. Though Isabella opposed harsh measures against the Jews on economic grounds, Torquemada convinced Ferdinand, and on 31 March 1492 the Alhambra Decree gave the Jews four months to leave, forbidding them to take gold, silver, money, arms or horses. It was long claimed that 200,000 left; Henry Kamen has argued that of about 80,000 Jews at most 40,000 left and the rest converted, and hundreds who stayed were investigated by the Inquisition. A Muslim uprising in 1499 was triggered by the monarchs' policy of forced conversions, and in 1502 they broke the Treaty of Granada and ordered Muslims to become Christians or leave.

She opposed the enslavement of the American natives, holding them subjects of the crown, though prisoners of war and those accused of cannibalism or sodomy could still be enslaved; when Columbus captured 1,200 men she ordered them returned and his arrest. Contemporaries such as the chronicler Hernando del Pulgar said she followed the path of rigour more than mercy. Antonio Rumeu de Armas argues that at Alcáçovas the monarchs bought peace at an excessively expensive price. Under the Catholic Monarchs the Cortes lost political power, becoming an almost passive body. Some authors claim that her reputation for sanctity derives largely from an image she shaped and spread herself.
sections.last:
Pope Alexander VI, whose conduct Isabella did not approve, granted her and Ferdinand the title of Catholic Monarchs. Her confessor Cisneros, named Archbishop of Toledo, reformed the religious institutions of Spain and, as chancellor, gained more and more power. In 1500 she granted all non-rebellious natives in the colonies citizenship and legal freedom by decree. Her court drew learned women, and she made Luisa de Medrano her protégée, who later taught Latin at the University of Salamanca. The monarchs tied Spain to Europe's dynasties: by 1497 their son John was married to Margaret of Austria, their daughter Isabella to Manuel I of Portugal and Joanna to Philip of Austria, and later Maria married Manuel and Catherine of Aragon married Arthur, Prince of Wales, and then Henry VIII.

Her plans for succession failed. Her mother died in 1496, her only son John in 1497 soon after his marriage, and her daughter Isabella in 1498 giving birth to Miguel da Paz, who died at two. Isabella declined after these deaths. She withdrew from government on 14 September 1504 and died on 26 November at the Royal Palace of Medina del Campo, of uterine cancer leading to dropsy. In her will she told her heirs not to allow the Indians "to receive any wrong in their persons and property". She was entombed in the Capilla Real in Granada beside Ferdinand, and her crowns passed to her daughter Joanna and Philip I.
sections.legacy:
Isabella and Ferdinand were the first monarchs to be called queen and king of Spain, and their marriage created the basis for its de facto unification. Their reign completed the Reconquista and began the Spanish Empire, which ultimately led to the creation of most of the nations of the Americas, and it opened the way to the Spanish Golden Age. Under her patronage Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba began a military career that changed the organisation and tactics of the Spanish army. Her reign also saw the dawn of the Spanish Inquisition. The monarchs' motto, "Tanto Monta", referred to their agreement as equal rulers.

Her contemporaries praised her: Andrés Bernáldez called her prudent, wise, chaste and devout, and Ferdinand declared in his testament that she was exemplary in every virtue. Her cause for sainthood was opened in 1958 by the Bishop of Valladolid, and a commission reported in 1970 that it had found no act of hers not inspired by Christian criteria; she was named Servant of God in 1974. In 1991 Pope John Paul II suspended the cause because of her expulsion of the Jews. The Spanish crown founded the Order of Isabella the Catholic in her honour in 1815, and in 1893 she appeared on United States stamps and coins for the four hundredth anniversary of Columbus's voyage. She has been portrayed in films, in the Spanish television series Isabel and in video games.

summary: Isabella I took the throne of Castile in 1474 after a civil war and a disputed succession, and with Ferdinand of Aragon reformed its finances and justice, conquered Granada and sponsored Columbus. Her drive for religious unity brought the Inquisition, the expulsion of the Jews and forced conversions of Muslims, and her cause for sainthood was suspended in 1991.

notes: The Veneration section calls Valladolid the place 'where she died'; the Death section gives Medina del Campo, used here.
The article does not give the Inquisition's founding date or any figures for its victims beyond the investigations after 1492; none given.
The claim that Isabella opposed harsh measures against the Jews 'on economic grounds' is stated without attribution in the article; kept as it stands.
Left out for want of room: the Segovia rebellion of 1476, which she rode into the city alone to end, and the birth of her son John in 1478.
